title: Comparing and Scaling
subtitle: Developing Proportional Reasoning in the Context of Number (Quantities)

aiPrompt.systemPrompt: You are a master middle school math teacher.
aiPrompt.mainPrompt: Below is a student's mathematics document, as a text summary, a picture, or both. Either may be absent. Evaluate and categorize it.
aiPrompt.categorizationDescription: Categorize the document based on its content and the general proportional reasoning curriculum found in middle grades mathematics.
aiPrompt.keyIndicatorsPrompt: Return exactly one item: a single sentence of at most 30 words, written to the student as "you", saying why this category fits by naming one specific thing in their document - a number, ratio, label, table column, or phrase they actually wrote. Do not restate the problem, summarize the document as a whole, or explain the mathematics in general.

sourceManifest.title: CSc 3.4 Leaky Faucets, Free Throws, Populations, and Environment

aiUnitSummary.overview: Comparing and Scaling is a grade 7 unit on proportional reasoning. Students compare quantities that subtraction cannot settle — which juice recipe tastes most orangey, which pizza company is cheaper, which team shoots free throws better — and build multiplicative strategies for doing so. Investigation 1 establishes ratio, equivalent ratios, scaling and unit rate, and names the proportion as an equation of two equal ratios. Investigation 2 moves to rates, separates proportional from non-proportional situations (a flat delivery fee breaks proportionality), and ties the unit rate to the constant of proportionality across tables, equations and graphs. Investigation 3 treats percent as a part-to-whole ratio scaled to 100, applied to sales tax, tips, and contexts with no money in them. Throughout, problems set several students' strategies side by side and ask which are valid and how they relate; additive comparison is repeatedly shown to be the wrong tool.

entries.priorKnowledge: From grade 6 Comparing Quantities: ratio as a multiplicative comparison of two quantities; equivalent ratios; part-to-part and part-to-whole forms; rate tables; percent as a part-to-whole comparison. From Stretching and Shrinking: ratios of corresponding lengths in similar figures. Students can write a ratio in words, with a colon and in fraction form, and know that multiplying or dividing both quantities by the same number leaves the comparison unchanged.
entries.problemDigest: Opens the unit with four orange-juice recipes of concentrate and water and asks which makes the most and least "orangey" juice. Students justify a ranking with part-to-part or part-to-whole comparisons, usually by scaling every recipe to a common amount of water, to a common amount of concentrate, or to a unit rate of water per cup of concentrate; percent appears as one option among several. The What If section shows five groups' work — scaling to 90 cups of water, a picture of concentrate spread across water, percents, scaling to 15 cups of concentrate, and one group subtracting the two quantities — and asks students to judge each and say how they are alike and different. The subtracting group is the unit's first explicit case of additive thinking failing where multiplicative thinking is required.
entries.approachGuidance: Students are asked to produce several valid comparison strategies and to evaluate other people's. Support more than one method rather than steering toward a single preferred one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratio as a multiplicative comparison; part-to-part and part-to-whole forms and the difference between them; unit rate as a ratio with one quantity scaled to 1, and that every ratio has two; scaling a ratio up or down to compare recipes, as established in 1.1; that comparing by subtraction gives the wrong answer.
entries.problemDigest: Returns to the four juice recipes and asks how much concentrate and water each needs for one cup of juice, and for 210 campers. Students scale by batches or work from a unit rate, often organising the work in a rate table with rows for concentrate, water and total juice. The What If section contrasts two strategies for reaching 210 cups — Aaliyah's rate table of equivalent ratios against Zaire's single equation 1/5 = x/210 — and asks how they are the same and different; a second situation scales a lemonade recipe to 160 ounces, requiring a unit conversion. This is where the rate table and the equation form of equivalent ratios are introduced as named strategies.
entries.approachGuidance: Students compare a table-based and an equation-based route to the same answer, and relate both to their own. Treat the strategies as alternatives to be understood, not ranked.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratios in part-to-part and part-to-whole form; equivalent ratios; unit rate; scaling by batches; rate tables and the equation form of two equal ratios from 1.2; ratios of corresponding sides in similar figures from Stretching and Shrinking.
entries.problemDigest: Names the proportion — an equation stating two ratios are equal — and the reasoning that uses it. Students apply it to four unrelated scenarios: sharing a smoothie bar in the ratio of two siblings' ages, converting a reading rate of 480 words in 3 minutes to a 20,000-word book and to an hour, finding a tree's height from similar triangles, and allocating student council seats at one representative per 30 students, where the division does not come out whole. The What If section asks whether Jayden's two different proportions for the reading problem are both correct (they are, giving 125 minutes), has students write a proportion for one of the other scenarios, checks a scale-factor argument for the trees, and asks whether the council allocation is fair — an opinion question about how to handle the remainder.
entries.approachGuidance: Several correct proportions exist for each scenario and students are asked to write their own and judge others'. Do not present one arrangement of the quantities as the right one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratio, equivalent ratios, scaling and unit rate; part-to-part and part-to-whole comparisons; the proportion as an equation of two equal ratios and proportional reasoning as the use of one; rate tables; that subtracting the two quantities in a ratio does not compare them.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces rate as a ratio comparing quantities in different units, with examples such as dollars per hour and grams of protein per serving. The challenge asks whether a camper at a ten-seat table with four pizzas gets the same amount as one at an eight-seat table with three, inviting several routes: scaling both to 40 people, to 12 pizzas, to pizza per person, or to people per pizza. The What If section presents three students — Selena's pizza-per-person, Tony's people-per-pizza, and Pedro's subtraction — where Tony scales correctly but misreads the result, since more people per pizza means less pizza each, and Pedro's difference has no meaning. Students then find how many pizzas 210 campers need at each table size, and design a ratio for a new 25-seat table.
entries.approachGuidance: The problem canvasses four or more ways to compare the two tables and asks students to decide which are sound. Help them evaluate a strategy rather than replace it.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratio, rate and unit rate; equivalent ratios and scaling; proportions and proportional reasoning; rate tables; part-to-part and part-to-whole comparisons; that a correct scaling can still be misread, and that differences do not compare ratios.
entries.problemDigest: Asks how to tell whether a situation is proportional at all. Julia compares two pizza companies: Royal charges a flat $13 per pizza, while Howdy's charges $11 per pizza plus a $30 delivery fee. Students complete a price table for each and choose a company for 84 pizzas. The What If section works through why Howdy's resists the usual methods — Amit scales the $195 for 15 pizzas without removing the delivery charge and gets the wrong unit price; Carlos sets up proportions and finds Royal's work and Howdy's do not; Meredith and Raffaele succeed by stripping the fee first, giving C = 13n against C = 11n + 30. Eun Mi and Prisha then graph both and notice Howdy's line does not pass through the origin, connecting the algebraic and graphical tests for proportionality.
entries.approachGuidance: Students examine four students' strategies and decide which hold for a non-proportional situation. Keep the focus on why a method fails here rather than on getting the number.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratio, rate, unit rate and equivalent ratios; proportions; rate tables; the test for a proportional relationship, including that its graph passes through the origin and its equation has no added constant; that a flat fee makes a pricing situation non-proportional.
entries.problemDigest: Names the constant of proportionality and identifies it with the unit rate. Oranges on sale at 10 for $2 are represented four ways at once — a rate table, a pair of proportions, two equations and two graphs — and students decide whether each is correct, what each says about the rate, and where the constant of proportionality appears in each. The two directions of the rate (cost per orange and oranges per dollar) are both represented, which is why there are two equations and two graphs but only one table. The What If section repeats this for concert tickets at $30 each, locating the constant in table, graph and equation, and uses each representation to find how many tickets $120 buys.
entries.approachGuidance: The point is that table, equation and graph each show the same constant. Move between representations rather than settling on one as the proper way to answer.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratio, rate, unit rate and the constant of proportionality; equivalent ratios, scaling, rate tables and proportions; tests for a proportional relationship across tables, equations and graphs; percent as a part-to-whole ratio scaled to 100, from grade 6.
entries.problemDigest: Opens the percent investigation by treating a sales-tax rate as a part-to-whole ratio with a whole of 100. Skylar has $25 and four items totalling about $24 with 5% tax, and students estimate the total, estimate the bill with tax, and decide whether he has enough — a question about whether their estimates were over or under. The What If section compares four strategies for adding 5% tax to an $8.95 notepad: Joseph multiplies by 0.05 and adds, Vanessa applies the distributive property to reach a single multiplication by 1.05, Amir extends a percent bar past 100% to 105%, and Leilani scales by 1.05. All are correct, and the discussion draws out that they are the same calculation seen four ways.
entries.approachGuidance: Four correct routes to the same total are compared, including estimation. Help students see how the methods relate instead of recommending one.

entries.priorKnowledge: Percent as a part-to-whole ratio with a whole of 100; adding a percent to a whole by multiplying by 1 plus the rate, and the percent-bar, proportion and distributive-property strategies from 3.1; unit rate and the constant of proportionality; scaling ratios.
entries.problemDigest: Applies percent twice over in one context. Groups build a lunch order from a menu, find the total including 6% sales tax, add a tip of between 15% and 20%, and divide the result equally among the group — so tax, tip and sharing compound, and the order of operations between them is the students' choice. The What If section teaches benchmark reasoning: Jabari finds 10% by shifting the decimal, halves it for 5%, and combines these for 15% or doubles for 20%; students apply this to two bills. A second situation works backwards from a $2.50 tip that is 20% of the bill to the bill itself, the unit's first reversal of a percent calculation.
entries.approachGuidance: Groups choose their own order and their own methods for tax, tip and sharing. Support the route a group has taken rather than imposing a standard sequence.

entries.priorKnowledge: Percent as a part-to-whole ratio scaled to 100; finding a percent of an amount and working backwards from a percent to the whole; benchmark percents; unit rate and the constant of proportionality in tables, equations and graphs; proportions and scaling.
entries.problemDigest: Moves percent away from money. Ming mixes chimpanzee food from high-fibre and high-protein sacks: a 40%/60% recipe for 225 scoops, then a reversal in which 30 scoops of high-protein food must be 40% of the adult mix, so the total is found by dividing rather than multiplying. The What If section gives the same recipe three representations — Ahmed's rate table, Mariana's pair of equations 0.4T = F and 0.6T = P, and Concetta's graphs — and asks how each shows the unit rate and how each lets Ming mix any quantity. The problem closes by asking what percents are good for, tying them back to tax, tip, markup and population change.
entries.approachGuidance: Table, equations and graphs are offered as three views of one recipe. Encourage movement between them rather than a single preferred representation.

entries.priorKnowledge: Ratio, rate, unit rate, percent and the constant of proportionality; proportions and scaling; rate tables, equations and graphs of proportional relationships; finding a percent of an amount and working backwards from one; that a percent is a ratio with a whole of 100 so two percents can be compared directly.
entries.problemDigest: Consolidates the unit across several unrelated settings. Students first run an experiment, dripping water from a punctured cup and recording volume at five-second intervals, then scale the measured drip rate to a day — their own data, so answers differ. The What If section then applies ratio reasoning to free-throw records of 108 of 126 against 195 of 257, where percents or a common quantity are needed to compare; to 2020 census data on the under-18 population, working backwards from a 1.4% decline and projecting it forward; and to further environmental comparisons. The closing question asks students to name proportional reasoning they meet in their own lives.
entries.approachGuidance: Students collect their own data and choose their own comparison methods across several contexts. Work from the data and strategy the student has rather than a model answer.

entries.priorKnowledge: The whole unit's content: ratio, rate, unit rate, percent and the constant of proportionality; equivalent ratios, scaling, rate tables, proportions, equations and graphs; how to decide whether a situation is proportional; and that proportional comparison is multiplicative, so differences between the quantities do not settle it.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's three Mathematical Reflections, one per investigation, each asking what it means to reason proportionally. Students are expected to articulate that proportional reasoning is multiplicative rather than additive; that ratios, rates, unit rates and percents all compare two quantities; that comparing requires relating the same two quantities in the same order, part-to-part or part-to-whole; that setting one quantity equal — including scaling to a whole of 100, or to 1 for a unit rate — is what makes two comparisons readable against each other; and that the constant of proportionality can be located in a table, an equation or a graph. This is a writing and discussion task with no new context.

entries.priorKnowledge: Whatever has been covered up to the point the exercises are assigned; the banks are organised by investigation and are normally used alongside the corresponding problems rather than after the whole unit.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's ACE question banks — Applications, Connections and Extensions exercises — collected as one item and grouped by investigation rather than taught as a problem. Investigation 1's bank repeats the mixture comparison with apple juice and asks students to judge written claims about which mix is most appley, several of which rest on additive reasoning. Investigation 2's bank covers sharing pizza across tables of different sizes, interpreting a reported ratio as a comparison rather than a count, and rate and price comparisons. Investigation 3's bank drills sales tax, tips and percent increase, including judging five different correct methods for the same tax calculation. Work here is individual practice on content introduced elsewhere in the unit.

investigations.title: CSc Investigation 1 Proportional Reasoning Using Ratio Comparisons

text: Problem 1.1 Mixing Juice: Choosing a Comparing Strategy

Students encounter an open-ended situation in which they need to make a decision using a comparison. In the Initial Challenge, students compare drink recipes using proportional reasoning to figure out which recipe will create the most “orangey” tasting juice. In the What If Situations they will analyze other student strategies for solving this challenge.
Describe some strategies for solving problems that involve ratios.

Use the Introduction to Investigation 1 to remind students of the mathematics in the Grade 6 Comparing Quantities Unit, including ratios, equivalent ratios, and unit rate. Review the definition of a ratio and the many ways that ratios can be written.

Introduce the orange juice recipes using Teaching Aid 1.1: Orange Juice Recipes. Tell students that Arvin and Mariah ask four people for help making the juice and each person gives them a different recipe.

• What do you notice about the orange juice recipes? What do you wonder?
  • Have you ever had juice or some other drink that tastes different depending on who makes it?
Help students connect prior learning to the recipes. Do not push for the comparison statements to be in any particular form.

Have different groups work on the different strategies in the What If Situations. This is an opportunity to provide for individual needs by have students work on strategies that can push their thinking in new directions.
After giving students some time to try a few ideas, you might suggest that students just begin by comparing two recipes rather than all four at once.

• Let’s take a look at Recipe A and Recipe B. Which do you think would be the most orangey?
  • How does the amount of water for Recipe A compare to the amount of water for Recipe B?
  • If we were looking at just water, how many batches of Recipe A would it take to get the same amount of water in Recipe B?
Some students will use naïve strategies such as simply focusing on the number of cups of concentrate and ignoring the water. Ask questions to challenge students’ ideas.

• How can we keep adding cups of water without making the juice less orangey?
  • What do you notice and wonder about the strategies in the What If?
  • Is this group using a part to part or part to whole way of thinking about the recipes?
  • Is this group using a strategy similar to something you did in Stretching and Shrinking or from the Grade 6 Comparing Quantities Unit?

As you are circulating during the Explore select student work to use in the Summary. Look for a variety of strategies to discuss and make connections. Find examples of part-to-part and part-to-whole thinking. Look for students using fractions, percents, unit rates, etc.

Have groups display their work. Then have students do a Gallery Walk to look at all of the work from other groups. Ask them what they notice and wonder about the strategies used by their classmates. As a class, discuss the strategies and solutions for determining which juice has the most orangey flavor.

As students explain, justify, and discuss the strategies in the What If to the whole class, ask questions to analyze the strategies. Also, compare the strategies to each other and to the strategies that your students used in the Initial Challenge.

• How did Moja’s, Lima’s, Tatu’s, or Sanji’s group think about this problem?
  • Is their thinking correct?
  • Why is Max’s strategy not a ratio?
  • Why do Stella, Elise and Dan have different unit rates?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

This Problem gives students the opportunity to practice the scaling strategies they explored earlier. The Initial Challenge goes back to the orange juice recipes from Problem 1.1. Students choose part-to-part or part-to-whole ratios, as appropriate. In the What If Situations students will look at scaling strategies to solve proportions, foreshadowing the next Problem, where proportions are defined and solving proportions is dealt with directly.
How do the strategies you used in this Problem compare to those used in Problem 1.1?

If students are not using the term “scaling ratios” from Stretching and Shrinking or Grade 6 Comparing Quantities, now is the time to encourage that vocabulary. Teaching Aid 1.2: Ratio Type Notation may be used to emphasize the scaling.
Use Learning Aid 1.2: Recipes to shift students’ attention back to the orange juice recipes. Have students consider making batches of each recipe for 210 campers.

• Arvin and Mariah are thinking about the supplies they need to make batches of juice. Does each recipe serve the same number of people?
  • Does this change how you will find the number of batches for each recipe?

• Are you using the recipe as a part-to-part or part-to-whole comparison? How did you decide?
  • Did you scale up a ratio? How did you decide what to multiply by? How do you know that the relationship between the ingredients is still correct?
  • How can you tell if two ratios are equivalent?
  • How could scaling help solve a problem? How can you decide on a scale factor to use?
  • How did each student in the What If Situations find equivalent ratios?
Look for student work examples to show using scaling strategies- rate tables, unit rates, proportions, etc.
The beginning of the Summary should be a time for students to share their strategies for finding the amount of supplies needed for making juice for 210 campers.

Choose groups of students who used different strategies. Have them explain why they think their ideas make sense and answer the questions. You want students to leave this Problem having experienced several problem-solving strategies and making connections between them.

• How are the strategies used in our classroom similar to and different from each other?
  • Do you have any What If questions?
  • How are Adia’s and Otis’s strategies alike? Different?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).
Problem 1.3 Keeping Things in Proportion: Using Proportions

In the Initial Challenge students encounter a variety of situations that involve proportional reasoning. In the What If Situations students will set up proportions and solve for unknown values. Students should start to formalize the process of setting up equivalent ratios that make similar comparisons of quantities. In particular, scaling one ratio to find an unknown value in an equivalent ratio is highlighted as one strategy to help find unknown values.
How are proportions like other strategies that you have used to solve ratio problems? How are they different?

Introduce the vocabulary of proportions and proportional reasoning. Revisit Adia’s and Otis’s strategies to introduce the terms from Problem 1.2. Ask students for examples of finding a missing quantity from prior Units. Teaching Aid 1.3 Proportional Reasoning Examples can be used to show a couple of examples from prior Units.

It is important that students understand that when setting up a proportion, the ratios are relating the same two quantities. Labeling the quantities will help students make sure that they are comparing.
Challenge students to answer the questions for each situation in the Initial Challenge. Make sure students know to show their work so strategies can be discussed in the Summarize.

Tell students that they are going to be working on a variety of situations where they need to find unknown values. Emphasize that they should find the unknown values using strategies you have discussed as a class (such as using equivalent ratios, rate tables, scaling, and writing proportions) and other strategies that make sense to them.

As students are working on the Initial Challenge and What If, check to see if they are using a variety of strategies to represent and solve the questions. Have students think about other ways to compare the quantities.

• For the various Situations and questions, are the ratios you are writing part-to-part or part-to-whole?
  • What are some strategies that you have heard for finding two equivalent ratios?
  • For What If Situation A, what strategies are you using to solve for x?
  • For Situation B, what would a proportion look like

As you are circulating during the Explore listen for students using the language of equivalent ratios and then how they use those to write and solve proportions. Find different examples of how students looked at the relationships in each context to compare- equivalent ratios, ratio tables, unit rates and proportions.
﻿Teacher Moves: Agency, Identity, Ownership; Compare Thinking

Select different groups to represent different strategies that you observed during the exploration. Consider taking one specific situation (or all, if you have time) and have students show multiple ways of solving the questions, such as using equivalent ratios, ratio tables, unit rates, and proportions. Encourage groups to explain how they got the answer and why the answer makes sense. Invite other students to question or challenge the solutions presented, to make connections between strategies, or to offer an alternative strategy.

Guide students’ thinking by asking them to think of other ways to set up the relationship. Help make explicit how the strategies for answering the questions are connected and how the proportions can be notated.

• Are there other ways of writing the same proportional situation?
  • Do you agree with the way that Nic wrote the proportions in the What If Situation A?
  • Which way of writing the proportion helps you to see the relationship between the quantities?
  • If we were to make a table for Reading Speeds, what might it look like?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

investigations.title: CSc Investigation 2 Proportional Reasoning Using Rate Comparisons

text: In the Initial Challenge two different numbers of pizzas are placed at tables that seat two different numbers of people. Students must determine whether this situation is fair. In the What If Situations students will analyze strategies such as finding how much pizza each person gets at the different tables, or how many people share a pizza. The numbers are small, so the comparison can be the central focus.
We have used several strategies for solving problems that involve ratios. How do you decide which method to use?
Remind students of the story about Arvin and Mariah making orange juice for campers in Problem 1.2. Let students know that you are going to consider another situation at the camp.
If you have the time, you may want to review some of the strategies that students used in Investigation 1 to solve problems, such as ratio tables and proportions.

For the Initial Challenge, have students keep their books closed or do not let them see the What If to start out. The What If presents student strategies that you may not want students to see until after working on the tables with pizzas. Introduce the Problem using Learning Aid 2.1A: Pizzas and Tables. You can use one Learning Aid per group. Tell students that the camp has a large table and a small table setup. They need to understand that the pizzas will be shared equally by everyone at the table and that a camper will be sitting at each plate.

• What do you notice about the tables and pizzas? What do you wonder?
  • What do you notice about the tables and pizzas? What do you wonder?
  • What quantities are being compared?
  • Will any of the strategies you used in Investigation 1 work for this situation?

This is an example of a ratio that relates quantities with different units, people and pizzas. After working through Investigation 1, most students should answer the Initial Challenge without too much difficulty, although some students may find it challenging to express their solutions in the language of ratios. It is possible to reason about the quantities and answer the question without finding specific numerical answers. As you walk around observing groups, push students to make their reasoning and conclusion visible to others.

• Do you think that your diagram, notations, and explanation will show another group how you are making sense of the question?
  • Can you think of another strategy to solve the Initial Challenge? Are your two strategies related? If so, how?

As you are circulating during the Explore look for the strategies students are using to solve this Problem to use during the Summary- pictures using estimation, how much pizza per person, how many people per pizza.

Students will come up with a variety of ways to reason about this Problem. Let them present their strategies to one another and justify the validity of their approaches. As students share their strategies, it is important to be clear about what comparisons are being made by the ratios. When students use certain strategies, such as scaling a ratio to an equivalent ratio, be sure to call attention to that strategy for the class. With unit rates, it is important for students to see how scaling a ratio so that one quantity is 1 connects to dividing to find a unit rate.
Strategies from students: (many examples given in the extended LES in the Teacher Guide)

• Reasoning with pictures and estimation
  • How much pizza for a fixed number of people
  • How many people for a fixed number of pizzas

• How much pizza for a fixed number of people.
  • How many people share a fixed number of pizzas
  • What quantities are you comparing? Do they have the same units of measure?
  • Since each ratio is a comparison of two quantities measured in different units (pizza and tables), they are called rates. Can you think of other rates that we have used?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

problems.title: CSc 2.2 Comparing Pizza Prices
problems.subtitle: How Do We Know It Is Proportional?

text: In Problem 2.2, students scale ratios to solve problems. The ratios in Problem 2.2 are rates. The Initial Challenge ratio/rate compares two quantities measured in different units, number of pizzas and price in dollars. In the What If Situations students will look at different strategies and representations to find rates and compare rate situations.
How can you determine if a situation is a proportional relationship?
Learning Aid 2.2: Royal and Howdy Pizza Costs
Use Learning Aid 2.2: Royal and Howdy’s Pizza Costs to discuss the comparison statements in the Introduction.

• Comparisons have two quantities. What are the two quantities in each statement?
  • Since each ratio is a comparison of two quantities measured in different units (number of pizzas and price in dollars), they are called rates. Can you think of other rates that we have used?
Use Teaching Aid 2.2: Introduction to review the rate table and proportion strategies in the Introduction. These strategies review finding the number of pizzas for 210 people in the previous Problem.

Introduce the Royal Pizza and Howdy’s Pizza deals using Learning Aid 2.2: Royal and Howdy’s Pizza Costs. You will want one Learning Aid per student to optimize class time. Tell students that Royal Pizza and Howdy’s Pizza are advertising their prices. Students need to notice the different costs for the different amounts of pizza.
• We are considering buying pizza for a class celebration. I found ads from two pizzerias. What do you notice and what do you wonder?

Be sure to hold a discussion after the Initial Challenge before moving on to the What If. This will allow you to highlight your students’ strategies before analyzing the strategies of other students that are presented in the What If.

• If we consider Royal Pizza, what do we know about the pizza costs there?
  • How might we draw a picture to represent that?
  • How does the $65 relate to the 5 pizzas?
  • How can we determine the cost of one of the pizzas?
  • For Royal, we know the cost for 5 pizzas. How can we find the cost for 10 pizzas?
  • For Howdy’s Pizza, if I look at the ad, it says that 15 pizzas cost $165. Why does the table show $195 for 15 pizzas?

Listen for how students are solving the Initial Challenge and how they decide that one company has pricing that is proportional and one does not. Listen for how students talk about the initial value of 0 versus 30 and how it impacts the situation. Select student groups to talk about the different representations and how they see when the situation is proportional.

Begin with a discussion of which pizzeria Julia should choose. This is an inequality situation. Groups should have different answers depending on the number of pizzas being considered. Push the students to consider when the price is better.

• How can you describe the pattern between the variables for Royal Pizza?
  • How can you describe the pattern between the variables for Howdy’s Pizza?

Have students share their strategies for finding the values on the tables. As students discuss their proportional reasoning with the tables, make sure to connect the various ways of notating their thinking. By the end of the discussion, students should connect finding the values in the tables to writing proportions. Students need to see that Royal’s rates are proportional and Howdy’s rates are not proportional.

• Does the scaling in Amit’s table work? Will 5 pizzas cost $65 at Howdy’s?
  • What do you think about Eun Mi’s claim in Situation A, do proportions work for Royal, but not for Howdy’s?
  • How do we find the unit rate?
  • How is this Problem similar to and/or different from previous Problems?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

problems.title: CSc 2.3 Finding Costs
problems.subtitle: Unit Rates and the Constant of Proportionality

text: Problem 2.3 Finding Costs: Unit Rate and Constant of Proportionality

This Problem focuses on how unit rate, or constant of proportionality, is helpful to solve problems. In the Initial Challenge students also look at the role of unit rate in different representations of tables, graphs, and equations with the context of buying oranges. The What If Situations continue this work with the contexts of buying tickets and pasta.

Describe how you can determine a unit rate, or constant of proportionality, from a description, rate table, equation, or graph? In what ways is a unit rate or the constant of proportionality helpful for solving a problem?
Graphing technology such as an online graphing program or a graphing calculator (optional)
If you did not introduce the vocabulary of constant of proportionality in the Summary of Problem 2.2, you can introduce the term now.

Students will be analyzing the proportionality in descriptions, tables, graphs, and equations. Let students know that the situation involves a sale on oranges where there are 10 oranges for $2. Students will analyze how they can use this information to think about buying any number of oranges. Have students begin this work independently for a few minutes and then work with a partner.
As groups work on this Problem, make sure that students are relating the two quantities in the rate table to the variables in the equations and graphs.

• What does the N stand for in the equations?
  • Where do you see number of oranges in the table? In the graph?
  • What does the C stand for in the equations?
  • Where do you see total cost in dollars in the table? In the graph?
  • In What if Situation A, what does the table, graph, or equation say to you?
  • For What if Situation B, is there a previous strategy that could help you?
Select student work for each representation to discuss how students found the unit rate or constant of proportionality.
Begin by having students discuss why Mia has only one table while she has two equations and two graphs.

• Why does Mia have only one table when she has two equations and two graphs?
  • What do Mia’s equations tell us?
  • What is the unit rate?
  • Where do you see the unit rate in the table? Equation? Graph?

• What is the unit rate or constant of proportionality for Noralie’s concert ticket?
  • Where do you see the constant of proportionality in the graph and the equation?
  • If I know that this is a proportional situation and 2 tickets cost $60, how can I find how many tickets I can buy with $120?
  • How are the representations (description, equation, graph, table) the same and different with a $10 processing fee?
  • How can we tell whether or not this is a proportional relationship?
  • For each store what if Mia did two divisions? 6 ÷ 7 = 0.857 and 7 ÷ 6 = 1.16666. What do the numbers tell us about the pasta at that store?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

investigations.title: CSc Investigation 3 Pulling it all Together: Ratios, Rates, and Percents

text: Problem 3.1 Using Percents: What is the Tax?

This Problem builds on students’ understandings of percent that began in the Grade 6 Comparing Quantities Unit. In the Initial Challenge students use the context of buying school supplies to explore the idea of tax. In the What If Situations students will look at multiple strategies for finding tax on those items, look at percent in general, and work backwards to find a total.
How are percent problems like ratio and rate problems?
Reasoning Proportionally with Quantities: Analysis and Synthesis
Learning Aid 3.1A Cost of Skylar’s School Items

Explain the use of percentages for discounts and taxes. It is important for students to understand that discounts take a percentage off of an amount and that taxes add a percentage to an amount. Some students may be familiar with this use of percentages.
Introduce the Skylar’s school items with tax using Learning Aid 3.1A: Cost of Skylar’s School Items.

• Why is it important to estimate?
  • How do we find estimates?
  • What is an estimate for the price of the sticky notes?
Then have students work on finding the exact costs with tax.

Be sure to hold a discussion after the Initial Challenge before moving on to the What If. This will allow you to highlight your students’ strategies before analyzing the strategies of other students that are presented in the What If.
As you move around the room, listen to students discuss the Problem. Find appropriate opportunities to ask students about connections among percents, ratios, and rates.
Encourage students to make their reasoning and conclusion visible to others. (See extended LES in Teacher Guide for student examples)

As you are circulating during the Explore look for examples of student strategies to use in the summary- percent bar or tape diagrams, double number lines, rate tables, informal proportions and proportions.
As a class, discuss the strategies and solutions for determining the total cost with tax.

• Does the estimate for the total bill with tax allow us to answer if Skylar will have enough money?
  • What are some ways that we can find the actual cost with tax?
For What If Situation A give students an opportunity to discuss how the five strategies are alike and how they compare to strategies that your students used to answer the questions.

• What strategy shows thinking like you did on the Initial Challenge?
  • Is there a strategy that you like and might use to answer questions in the future?
  • Whose strategies look different but are really using the same type of reasoning?
The student wonderings in What If Situation B push students to connect their current thinking to previous mathematical ideas.

• Do you agree with Sam or Will?
  • Do you agree with Nicky or Marta? Is there more than one price with tax? Or is it the same to find tax on each item and the tax on the total of the items?
Given the tax amount and percentage, students have to determine the whole in What If Situation C. Push students to relate this to previous strategies discussed in class.
• How could I use a (choose some strategy, such as rate table) to find out how much Funda paid for the used gaming system?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).
Problem 3.2 Using Percents: What is the Tip?

The goal of this Problem is to give students more practice in solving the standard family of percent problems. In the Initial Challenge the context is calculating tax, and tips (or service charges) on restaurant meals. In the What If Situations students will look at multiple strategies for tax, tips, and discounts.
Describe some strategies you used to solve percent problems.

If students do not eat out or usually eat out only at fast food restaurants, they might not be familiar with tipping. It might be useful to explain how that system works and even to work out one simple example as a whole class.
• Suppose you eat at a restaurant and the bill comes to $14. What would a tip of 10% be? A tip of 20%? A tip of 15%? ($1.40; $2.80; $2.10)
Following up on the strategies from Problem 3.1, you might ask:
• Can you show how to work out these tips on a percent bar? Rate table? Writing a proportion?
Alert students that the questions here are about tips and discounts, but the same kind of reasoning as in Problem 3.1 will apply. Encourage them to use tape diagrams, rate tables, or proportions.

The openness of the Initial Challenge is an inviting opportunity for students to make their own choices. Time will be a factor when sharing their work in the Summary. You may want to have groups do a Gallery Walk. Have each group put their work on large chart paper to use in a Gallery Walk in the Summary.
Implementation Note: You may want to use a menu from a local restaurant instead of Larry’s Lunch Place.

• How did you calculate the bill plus tax?
  • How did you calculate your share of the bill?
  • Would it have given you the same answer if you divided the total bill by 4, then divided the tip by 4, and then added?

Select student strategies to highlight in the Summary to help students make connections between the different strategies: percent bar or tape diagrams, double number lines, rate tables, informal proportions and proportions.
During the Gallery Walk, you can have groups rotate to at least two other groups’ work. Students can check the work and give feedback on sticky notes.
• Some groups found the sub-total for the food items and then added 6% of that amount to the bill. How else might you calculate the total amount?
Use the What If Situations to make sure that all students have strategies for finding percents such as tax, tips, and discounts.

• What happens when we find 10% of a number?
  • How can I use the 10% rate to find the 20% rate?
Use What If Situation B to make sure that all students have strategies for finding the quantity of 100% when a percentage and quantity are given.
• In What If Situation C, did you use the same strategy or did you change your strategy when finding the 6% tax then finding the 15% tip?

What If Situation D explores what happens when you have discounts on top of discounts. This is often counterintuitive for students. Many will think that this is an application of the Distributive Property, but it is not.
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

The mathematics in this Problem reviews and connects the three main proportional reasoning focuses of this Unit: ratios, rates, and percents. Like the orange juice problem earlier in the Unit, students are presented with a mixture context. In the Initial Challenge students will be answering questions about food mixtures for baby chimps. In the What If Situations students will look at multiple strategies for solving these mixture situations and then apply them with adult chimp food recipes.
How are percents useful to solve problems?

This Problem is intended to bring together the proportional reasoning of ratio, rate, and percent. It may be a time to revisit a few previous Problems from each Investigation. You may want to look back at Summary notes or anchor charts where you kept track of what students were taking away from the Problems. Problems to revisit might include: Problem 1.2 Mixing Juice, Problem 2.1 Sharing Pizzas, Problem 2.2 Comparing Pizza Prices, and Problem 3.1 Using Percents. For your class, there may be different Problems that resulted in reflective moments on the mathematical highlights.

For the Initial Challenge, have students keep their books closed or look only at the Initial Challenge. The What If portion of the Problem presents student strategies that you may not want students to see until after working on the baby and adult chimp mixture questions in the Initial Challenge.
Introduce the chimp recipes using Learning Aid 3.3: Chimp Food Mixtures. You can use one Learning Aid per group of two students.

You may want to hold a discussion after the Initial Challenge before moving on to the What If. This will allow you to highlight your students’ strategies before analyzing the strategies of other students that are presented in the What If. You can use the strategies in the What If to connect to how your students thought about the proportional reasoning in the chimp food questions.

• What could be a comparison statement for how to make the mixture for baby chimps?
  • Is this part-to-part or part-to-whole?
  • What would be a comparison statement for the total of the mixture for baby chimps?
  • Is this part-to-part or part-to-whole?
  • What is a unit rate we could find for the Baby Chimp mixture?
  • Why is finding unit rate helpful?
  • What are some other strategies that we have used in this Unit to help answer proportional questions like these?
Students should be able to draw on their experiences in this Unit and reference tip, tax, mixtures when the quantities aren’t equal, etc.
Have students show and discuss their strategies for answering the chimp recipe questions.
Help students connect the way they chose to answer the questions to other strategies in What If Situation A.
Choose a strategy that connects to the strategies that your students used in class.

• How does this strategy compare to yours?
  • What strategies did Ms. Stewart’s class use that we did not? How are those strategies useful?
  • How are the two representations in What If Situation B related?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

problems.title: CSc 3.4 Leaky Faucets, Free Throws, Populations, and Environment
problems.subtitle: What’s the Connection?

text: Problem 3.4 Leaky Faucets, Free Throws, Populations, and Environment: What’s the Connection

This Problem provides students with an opportunity to further develop their understanding of proportional relationships. In the Initial Challenge students will simulate a leaky faucet using a paper cup with a hole in it that is dripping water. In the What If Situations students will encounter various contexts involving ratios and be given representations to create their own contexts and question.
Describe some situations that you encounter in your daily life that require proportional reasoning.
Timer or clock with a second hand
Clear measuring containers that measure milliliters (such as a graduated cylinder)
Discuss student work in this Unit using rates, rate tables, and unit rates.

• When have we used rates in this Unit?
  • When have we used rate tables in this Unit?
  • When have we used unit rates in this Unit?
Explain the situation using the Introduction about leaky faucets wasting water every year.
Have students work in groups of 3-4 to collect their data and then complete the Problem. Distribute Learning Aid 3.4: Leaky Faucet Data for students to record their data from the simulation.
You may want to give each group two of the situations from What If Situation A to differentiate based on needs of each group
Have groups do What If Situation B on large paper so that it can be used in a Gallery Walk in the Summary.

Implementation Note: This Problem may take two days to complete the experiment, analyze the data, and complete the Problem. You may want to hold a brief summary after the Initial Challenge and have students complete the What If on the second day.
As groups are working on the leaky faucet simulation, monitor that they are following the directions to get adequate data.

• Is the hole in their cup small enough? Is the hole clogging up?
  • Are they collecting data every 5 seconds?
  • Are they continuing to add water as the cup empties? (Keeping about the same amount of water in the cup at all times)
  • Are they accurately reading the container catching the water?
Some students may need assistance when looking at the contexts in What If Situation A.

• What is the ratio/rate in this situation?
  • What are some strategies we have used in this Unit that might help you?
As you are circulating during the Explore listen for conversations students are having about the given contexts and about the contexts they create for What If Situation D.
Have students share their results from the Leaky Faucet Experiment. Have students share how they used this data to make predictions in the Initial Challenge.
Have students discuss the Situations in What If Situation A.
Have students display their work for What It Situation B in a Gallery Walk.
• How did you use your data to make predictions in the Initial Challenge?
In What If Situation A, discuss the ratio application(s).

• What is the ratio in this application?
  • How did you use the ratio to answer the questions in this application?
  • What are some ways that we can answer these questions?
During the Gallery Walk for What If Situation B have students look at two or more other posters and decide if they agree or disagree with the posters.
• Do you agree with the posters you looked at? Why or why not?
As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

Comparing and Scaling Mathematical Reflection

The Mathematical Reflection provides an opportunity to discuss the goals of the Investigation. Students can pull together their reasoning from the Now What Do You Know questions to summarize their learning over the time.

Students can record their responses to the Mathematical Reflection to create a record of their current understandings of the big ideas of the Unit. The Mathematical Reflection can provide a self-assessment for students. Each student can have check points of their understanding of the mathematics after each Investigation.

Students can use the MR to consolidate their mathematical thinking, take notes, and provide evidence of what they know and can do.

A teacher can gain an understanding of student thinking during a discussion of the reflection question. Then one can assess individual understanding based on each student’s written work.

Mathematical Reflection

What does is mean to reason proportionally?

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

Teacher Moves: Time

Having students refer to their notes from the Now What Do You Know in each Problem in the Investigation can help them to synthesize all their ideas around proportional reasoning.

As a class discuss the Mathematical Reflection. Sample strategies to have students synthesize and record their thinking are listed in the EXPLORE section.

Suggested questions

  • After this Investigation, what do we know about proportional relationships between two variables?
  • What did we learn in each Problem of this Investigation?
  • How might we describe the “big mathematical idea(s)” of the Investigation?

EXPLORE

Teacher Moves: Anchor Chart, Portrayal, Language

Example Strategies for Student Participation

A few creative strategies teachers use to encourage students' ownership of their learning.

Anchor Charts

After a discussion, chart the emerging understanding and post it in the classroom. This can be done on poster paper or electronically.

  • Work with students throughout the unit to reference, add to, or refine their understandings.
  • Note: For teachers who move classrooms or have multiple classes of the same grade level, create the chart in all classes, but keep just one represent all of your classes. Post this one in the room or bring it out when needed.

Note Organization

Some teachers use the Mathematical Reflections as an organizer for note taking during the Investigation.

  • As part of the Summarize of the Problems, students record key ideas to the Now What Do You Know? reflection questions on a separate paper.
  • At the close of the Investigation, students synthesize their notes into responses that summarize their emerging understandings of the ideas in the unit.

Word Bank

As a class, create a word bank of terms from the Investigation.

  • Have groups of students write 3 – 4 statements using the words from the bank.
  • After formatively assessing their statements, you may choose to have a class discussion to refine the statements.

Chalk Talk

With a chalk talk, your writing does “the talking” instead of talking aloud.

  • Post the question(s) on sheets of chart paper or on sections of your board
  • Small groups record responses while collaborating in “chalk talk” format
  • Students move to others’ work and add their thinking in the form of new ideas and connections

Final Reflection Presentation

Teachers sometimes use the MR after the last Investigation as a summary of students’ learning.

  • Students consolidate their learning from the Unit.
  • Teachers choose from various ways to present their ideas. Presentation choices might include creating a: Poster, Written Paper, PowerPoint/Prezi, Song/Rap, etc.

Partner Write

Students create a written response to the reflection question with a partner.

  • Students discuss the reflection question with a partner.
  • Students create and write a response with a partner.

SUMMARIZE

Student Responses

At the beginning of the year, students will need more collaboration to outline and summarize the important ideas. They may need examples of writing, diagrams, and/or justifications from other students to help build their vision of what is expected when answering a Mathematical Reflection. Early in the year you may want to start writing Mathematical Reflections as a whole group. Then as the year progresses, move to small groups, pairs, and finally individuals.

Each Investigation contributes to students’ conceptual understandings of the ideas in the Unit. Students’ explanations at the beginning of a Unit might be just forming. As you progress through the Unit, students can use the contexts, representation, and connections to express a more solid understanding. By the end of the Unit, students can create a complete picture of understanding.
